32.srule: None: the Compendio defines the Aymara word as a sequence of phonemes carrying a single, non-phonemic stress on the penultimate vowel of the complete word (Cap. II §2.4 p. 22; Cap. III §2.21 p. 44 'un acento principal'); Cap. III §2.2-2.21 describes no other stress. For the Chilean altiplano variety, Poblete & Salas 1997:149-150 likewise state none inside the simple word: 'todas las sílabas... se pronuncian con aproximadamente la misma longitud, intensidad y altura de tono, excepto la penúltima... y la última'; each member of a compound or reduplication keeps its own penult prominence (qa.la.qa.la 3-1-3-1).

morph.rootq: Ch. III §2.2 'Acento' p.43 (Laura Martin): 'El acento en aymara no es fonémico, cayendo siempre sobre la penúltima vocal. ... Después de realizar toda sufijación y la correspondiente supresión morfémica de vocales dentro de la palabra (ver Capítulo IV), el acento se coloca sobre la penúltima vocal de la forma completamente sufijada.' p.44: 'A causa de que el acento no es fonémico y cae sólo en una posición específica, puede cambiarse de vocal en vocal de acuerdo al incremento en la longitud de la palabra mediante el proceso de sufijación. Por ejemplo ... [kuláka] /kullaka/ 'hermana' ... por adición del sufijo /–xa/ 'mi' se vuelve [kulakáxa] ... [kulakaxámpi] ... [kulakaxampíwa]'. Also Ch.…
morph.elicq: Ch. III §0 p.25 (data statement for the phonology chapter that contains the stress section): 'Los datos para esta descripción también vienen de unas cien horas de investigación y análisis basadas en listas de palabras, varios textos cortos y numerosas conversaciones. Además se incluyen dos minutos de una narración grabada, una lista de vocabulario de mil palabras y las cintas de instrucción en idioma aymara ...'. The stress section itself (§2.2 p.43) illustrates with a sentence: 'en una frase tal como /jupáx yapúr saríwa/ 'él/ella fue a la chacra' ... Luego pueden aplicarse reglas que actúan a nivel de frase para suprimir vocales finales de palabra'. No instrumental measurement is reported…
morph.stmt: Ch. II §1 p.16: 'El aymara es un idioma sufijante del tipo que a menudo se llama sintético o polisintético.' and Ch. II §2.2 p.21: 'Las clases morfológicas básicas son raíces y sufijos. Las raíces son morfemas simples que ocurren inicialmente en las palabras.' — i.e. exclusively suffixing: root-initial words followed by derivational, inflectional (portmanteau person/tense), independent and sentence suffixes; no prefixes.

morph.rootq: Širaliev 1997 §2.1.2 p.162 (translated from Russian): 'Словесное ударение в А.я. является экспираторным. Долгота гласного в слове не находится в зависимости от ударения. В исконных именах ударение обычно падает на конечный слог многосложного слова, тогда как в спрягаемых формах глагола, деепричастиях и наречиях, в зависимости от характера аффиксов, ударение может приходиться не на конечный слог. Некоторые служебные слова, а также аффиксы сказуемости, глагольного отрицания и некоторые другие являются безударными, например: ушаг үчүн 'для ребенка', јазычы́јам 'я писатель', көрү́рсән 'видишь', де́мә 'не говори'.'…
morph.elicq: Širaliev 1997 gives no indication of the evidence base for the stress statement (encyclopaedic sketch of the literary language; §2.1.2 simply asserts 'Словесное ударение в А.я. является экспираторным ... ударение обычно падает на конечный слог многосложного слова' with isolated example words). The catalog's stress reference, Mokari & Werner 2017 (JIPA), likewise states the stress rule without saying how it was established; its data description concerns the passage and vowels only: 'The transcription of the reading passage is based on the speech of a 28-year-old male native speaker who was born and raised in Tabriz ... The vowel plot is based on recordings from 20 male and 23 female native…
morph.stmt: Širaliev 1997 §2.3.0 p.163: 'Морфологический тип А.я. агглютинативно-синтетический' [the morphological type of Azerbaijani is agglutinative-synthetic]; §2.5.1 p.168: 'Типичная структура словоформы в А.я. такова: корневая морфема всегда занимает начальную позицию в производном слове, за ней следует аффикс словообразования, далее следуют аффиксы функционально-грамматических форм и морфологических категорий (для имени — аффиксы мн. числа, принадлежности, падежа, сказуемости; для глагола — аффиксы отрицания, наклонения, времени, лица-числа и др.); конечную же позицию как в имени так и глаголе занимают аффиксы-энклитики, выступающие в функциях вопросительных, условных и модальных частиц…

corr.detail: Dunn 1988:34: in four- and five-syllable words the only secondary stress is on the third syllable, final syllables are never stressed, and no words of more than five syllables are extant. Badimaya is therefore withdrawn as an attestation of the Maranungku pattern; it belongs instead to the family with binary alternation that leaves the final syllable unstressed.

34.dq: Primary stress is initial, as in: /wanara/ long, thin /windyindyi/ grasshopper. In words of four or five syllables, a weaker secondary stress occurs on the third syllable from the front: /ngan.ganguwa/ to choke on something /wanaldyilinga/ scorpion. This suggests an alternating stress pattern ... Unfortunately, no words of more than five syllables, necessary to test this hypothesis, are extant.
34.prule: Primary stress on the initial syllable of the word.
34.srule: Secondary stress (weaker) on the third syllable in words of four or five syllables; Dunn's rule (2) places secondary stress on every second syllable after a stress provided another syllable follows, so final syllables are never stressed; no words longer than five syllables exist to test the alternation further.

morph.rootq: §2.3, pp.33-34: 'Primary stress is initial, as in: /wanara/ long, thin; /windyindyi/ grasshopper. In words of four or five syllables, a weaker secondary stress occurs on the third syllable from the front: /ŋan.gaŋguwa/ to choke on something; /wanaldyiliŋa/ scorpion. This suggests an alternating stress pattern that might be described by the following rules: (1) $ -> primary stress / # __ (2) $ -> secondary stress / $[+stress] $ __ $.' The rules are stated over the word (word-initial syllable, third syllable), with no reference to root, stem or suffix; note the illustrating form ŋan.ga-ŋguwa carries its secondary stress on the present-tense suffix -ŋgu-.
morph.elicq: No method is stated; the stress claim is illustrated only with isolated citation words and closes: 'Unfortunately, no words of more than five syllables, necessary to test this hypothesis, are extant.' (p.34). The grammar as a whole rests on elicitation from a single rememberer: 'This grammar is an attempt to salvage as much information as possible on Badimaya, on the basis of data collected from one speaker of the language, Mr Joe Benjamin.' (Abstract, p.19).
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing: 'A Badimaya word consists of a base stem, usually augmented by one or more derivational and/or inflectional suffixes.' (§2.4.4, p.37); 'All verb forms consist minimally of a verb stem plus an inflectional suffix, except the imperative form, which is identical to the uninflected stem' (§4, p.82); the only preposed elements are body-part nouns in N+V compounds (dyina-yara foot-go 'to walk', §4.5 p.98) and leftward reduplication.

corr.detail: The word-level trochaic coding (stress on odd-numbered syllables from the left) is exact for words of up to four syllables. Words of five or more syllables are polymorphemic, with juncture accents described as "always dactylic", so the odd-numbered-syllable pattern coded for five- to eight-syllable words is a projection rather than an attested fact.

morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing (with enclitics): nominal word 'STEM + NUMBER + POSSESSIVE + CASE. The case marker is thus always final in the nominal word' (III.1.4 p.53, Hercus placing Bagandji among 'the suffixing languages of Australia'); verbal word 'Verb stem ± Vb ± Voice ± ASP + Tense ± Sub ± Obj ± DAT... The order of morphemes is strictly adhered to' (V.1.1 pp.175-176); clitics 'in Bagandji they are always enclitic to a preceding word' (VI.1.1 p.219). No prefixes are described anywhere; negation and interrogation use free sentence-initial words.

36.tone: The second cited description (English typescript 'Notes on Phonetics of Bagirmi', pp. 16-17, §(3) Intonation; identified by StressTyp2 and this record with Stevenson 1969) analyses Bagirmi as tri-tonal (High, Mid, Low) and lists tonal doublets to be distinguished, including kag(a) 'tree' vs kaga 'leopard' — the pair Gaden 1909:8 treats as an accent-class contrast (kag/a vs kaga); it makes no stress or accent statement. dfl.q: Stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and invariably so when the second syllable contains a semi-mute vowel. A phonological word is defined as a sequence of at least two syllables in which primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable. Suffixation perturbs primary stress to the right according to the number of syllables affixed. Such affixation is considered part of the phonological word: ['kol.lo?] /kollo?/ 'to remove', [kol.'lo.?in] /kollo?in/ 'remove it', [kol.lo.'?an.ku] /kollo?anku/ 'I will remove it'. Monosyllabic particles ... do not carry stress of their own and do not perturb the stress of the preceding word; therefore, they are not considered a part of the preceding phonological word.'…
morph.elicq: Gault 1979 gives no statement of how stress was determined; the stress section cites isolated words and short verb+clitic/particle strings (/kollo?/, /kollo?in/, /kollo?anku/, /?amangan pa ?aku/ 'I will eat yet', /kulang da/ 'only a little'), and Note 1 p.65 says only: 'This paper is a result of an analysis of data gathered in the barrio of Panigayan during 1975 and 1976 under the auspices of the Summer Institute of Linguistics. It builds upon the analysis begun by Eunice Diment and uses much of the data gathered by her.' Stress is also used diagnostically elsewhere ('the penultimate stress pattern indicates that the following word has three syllables, not four', §1.4.2 p.55), again on…
morph.stmt: Predominantly prefixing (with one infix): Gault 1999 §2.2.7 p.22 'With the exception of BF and imperatives, Bangingi' affixes are prefixed to the root' in the order mode + focus + aspect + causation + root (e.g. maka-pag-pa-bowa 'was able to send back and forth'), and Gault 1979 §2.2.4 p.64 'There are three suffixes in Baangingi, all vowel-initial: /-an/, /-in/, and /-un/'; post-root material is otherwise limited to the referential enclitic -in and cliticized ergative/possessor pronouns, while case, plural and negation are free preposed particles.

37.exc_quote: [Gault 1979 §1.3 p. 54] Monosyllabic particles comprise a separate category of morphemes. They do not carry stress of their own and do not perturb the stress of the preceding word; therefore, they are not considered a part of the preceding phonological word. In the examples below, pa and da are the particles. [ʔʌ.ˈma.nʌŋ pa ˈʔa.ku] /ʔamaŋan pa ʔaku/ 'I will eat yet', and [ˈku.lʌŋ da] /kulaŋ da/ 'only a little'.

38.srule: Secondary stress falls on the initial syllable of the phonological word when two syllables precede the penultimate primary stress ([bòlusúkon] 'durian', [mòroʔóne] 'male'); verbal prefixes form a separate, more weakly stressed phonological word, so a prefixed trisyllable has initial secondary stress ([nìmbéla]) while a single-morpheme trisyllable does not ([bakókoʔ]), and with two prefixes the secondary falls on the first prefix ([màmpapatéi], [nòtontokúi]).
38.quote: The phonological word is defined here as the domain of word stress. The phonological word (PW) may be one or more syllables (S), and can be summarized as follows for polysyllabic forms: PW = ((S̀) S) Ś S The phonological word is normally disyllabic and, as such, receives penultimate primary stress (´). The stressed syllable may typically be preceded by one or two syllables; if two, the initial syllable receives a secondary stress (`). ... Suffixes, however, unlike prefixes, are pulled into the stress pattern of the verb base and count as the ultimate syllable.

We have not carried out any acoustic analysis of these prosodic features and our statements must, therefore, be considered…
morph.stmt: §3.2 (p. 25): 'Morphologically, the language is rich, making use of prefixes, infixes, suffixes, circumfixes and several types of reduplication'; the affix-order tables (§5.8, Tables 5.5-5.7, pp. 119-120) give up to four prefix slots (voice/mode mVng-/nVng-/pVng-, ni-, attemptive, requestive, causative, stem formers) and up to five suffix slots (applicatives -i/-ii/-kon, PV.I -on, LV -an, possessive/agent suffixes, enclitics -mo/-si/-po) around the root, i.e. mode/voice and derivation are predominantly prefixal (plus infixes -um-, -in-) while possession, agent indexing, applicatives and aspectual enclitics are suffixal; nouns take no case, number or definiteness affixes.

38.sec_rule: Secondary stress on alternating syllables to the left of the penultimate primary stress (van den Berg & Busenitz 2012:13 §2.7, e.g. mà.tang.kú.mo 'it is my eye'). The primary source, Busenitz & Busenitz 1991:29-31 and p. 45 n. 4, placed a single secondary stress word-initially: on the first of two pretonic syllables of a monomorphemic phonological word ([bòlusúkon] 'durian') and on the first prefix of a prefixed verb, even a trisyllabic one ([nìmbéla] 'wounded', [màmpapatéi] 'to kill').
38.sec_quote: if two, the initial syllable receives a secondary stress (`). ... a single prefix, or a combination of prefixes together, function, for stress purposes, as independent--but more weakly stressed--PW's. Therefore, a three-syllable word containing a prefix would have secondary stress while a single-morpheme three-syllable word would not.

39.sec_rule: None in ordinary words: 'I could not discern, nor elicit, secondary stresses' (even five-syllable katiwawalan [katiwawa'lan] has one stress); a second stress occurs only in reduplicated words, on the final syllable of each copy (gigi ['gi'gi], lumbalumba [lum'bəlum'bə]), and moves to a suffix if one is added (lumbalumba-ne [lumbalumba'ne]). Clynes asks native analysts to check secondary stress in particular (fn. 18).
39.sec_quote: I could not discern, nor elicit, secondary stresses. ... Where a word is inherently reduplicated, it carries two stresses; stress is therefore assigned before reduplication, in the lexical phonology: (60) gigi ['gi'gi] 'tooth' ... lumbalumba [lum'bəlum'bə] 'dolphin' ... However, complex morphemes like katiwawalan (4.1), or dumalada (6.1.1), carry only a single stress. I conclude that the only relevant stress-bearing unit is the rightmost syllable in the phonological word.

43.dq: Stress is generally post-initial, i.e., on the second syllable of the word, although some exceptional words show initial stress.
43.dloc: Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003:102 (archive.org scan, verifier; note on the cited source)
43.heavy: none: the source states no syllable-weight criterion (no long-vowel, closed-syllable or vowel-quality condition) for any Basque accentual type. The only rime-referencing wording is the hedged Standard-Basque capsule 'Bisyllabic words ending in a vowel receive initial stress instead' (p. 65); the same rule is stated positionally on p. 71 ('accent retraction to the initial syllable in bisyllabic forms') and p. 102 ('When the second syllable is word-final... stress is retracted to the first syllable') with consonant-final gí.zon 'man' retracting alongside mén.di, bú.ru.
43.dflt: not applicable (no weight criterion); general rule = second syllable, initial in bisyllabic forms
43.prule: Central accentual type (most of Gipuzkoa, parts of Bizkaia and Navarre; also the dominant Standard-Basque pattern): postinitial accent = second syllable of the word, retracted to the initial syllable when the second syllable would be word-final (bisyllables); a lexical class of exceptional words (borrowings, compounds, béstea, égia...) takes initial accent; in some varieties short plurals take initial accent. Other dialect types in the same source: Northern Bizkaian = lexical pitch-accent (most words unaccented and prominent only phrase-finally; accented stems and pre-accenting suffixes give H*L on a nonfinal syllable, first accent wins; Lekeitio shifts all accents to the penult); Western Gipuzkoa (Antzuola/Bergara) = word-penultimate, stem-penultimate in plurals; Zuberoan = penultimate with a marked contrastive oxytone class; Baztan (N. High Navarrese) = penultimate. StressTyp2's Basaburua-Imoz passage (< Hualde 1999, carried): primary on the first or second syllable in the singular, on the plural-suffix syllable in the plural.
43.srule: Standard Basque: frequently a secondary prominence on the last syllable of the word or phrase, with the main stress on the second syllable (alábarentzat dà 'it is for the daughter', lagúnarì 'to the friend') — Hualde 2003:65, hedged 'frequently'. Hualde 1997:143-144 states the condition for the same pattern: a secondary accent on the final syllable when at least one unstressed syllable precedes it (words of four or more syllables under [+2]). No secondary stress is mentioned for the central dialectal type (sec. 2.2.3, p. 71) or for Tolosa (Elordieta, sec. 2.3.2.1, pp. 102-104).
43.quote: [p. 71] In a large central area covering most of Gipuzkoa and parts of Bizkaia and Navarre, the general rule is postinitial accent (on the second syllable), with some exceptional words receiving, instead, initial accent. The general pattern is illustrated by examples such as gizóna 'the man', gizónari 'to the man', gizónarena 'the one of the man', txistúlaria 'the flutist', txistúlariari 'to the flutist'. 43.cfw: Hualde's accent chapter in the 2003 Mouton reference grammar, his 1997 monograph on Basque accentuation, the 2015 acoustic study by Gandarias, Gaminde, Unamuno and Iglesias of a Standard-Basque speaker and Munarriz's 2006 study of an Ataun speaker all put the default accent on the second syllable of the word in Standard and central Basque, while the lexical pitch-accent systems of Northern Bizkaian (Elordieta and Selkirk 2018, Ito 2002, Wolf 2008) and the penultimate accent of the eastern dialects (Hualde 1997) are other dialects, not disagreements about this record. Souletin is described separately below, with a different pattern.

variants.name: Souletin (Zuberoan) Basque
variants.prule: General rule: penultimate accent (paroxytonic). Marked oxytonic (final) accent in: (a) absolutive singular of -a stems (historical /a+a/ contraction: alhabá vs uninfl. alhába); (b) all plural forms except the absolutive (gizunék, gizunér vs ABS PL gizúnak); (c) words with certain monosyllabic derivational morphemes when uninflected (aitañí); (d) a group of monomorphemic lexical exceptions (arrés, animál). Accent is contrastive.
variants.quote: 2.2.4. Zuberoan. Zuberoan is the only eastern dialect with contrastive accent. The general accentual rule of Zuberoan is penultimate accent, as seen in table 40. [Table 40. Zuberoan: General paroxytonic pattern: gízun 'man', gizúna 'the man, ABS', gizúnak 'the men, ABS or the man, ERG'; bezála 'like', bezaláko '(of) like', bezalakóxe '(of) like, DIM'] However, there is also a marked oxytonic pattern. In some cases, oxytonic accent is clearly the result of a historical contraction. For instance, the absolutive singular form of stems ending in -a, where a historical sequence /a+a/ has been reduced, shows final accent, table 41 (a). Final accent is also found in plural forms of all words, except in the absolutive. To explain this case a historical contraction has also been proposed, table 41 (b). [Table 41. Zuberoan: Exceptional oxytonic pattern: (a) alhabá 'the daughter, ABS' < *alhaba-a, cf. uninfl alhába; neská 'the girl, ABS' < *neska-a, cf. uninfl néska; (b) gizunék 'the men, ERG' < *gizon-ag-ek; gizunér 'to the men, DAT' < *gizon-ag-er(i), cf. uninfl gízun, ABS PL gizúnak] Words bearing certain monosyllabic derivational morphemes also present final stress when uninflected (e.g. aitañí 'grandfather', cf. áita 'father'). There is also a group of monomorphemic words which exceptionally present final instead of penultimate stress (e.g. arrés 'sheep', animál 'huge').
variants.cite: Hualde, José Ignacio. 2003. 'Accentuation' (section 2.2), in J. I. Hualde & J. Ortiz de Urbina (eds.), A Grammar of Basque (Mouton Grammar Library 26), Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter; section 2.2.4 'Zuberoan', pp. 71-72.
variants.cfw: Hualde (1997, 2003), Gaminde (1995) and Egurtzegi & Elordieta (2023) all describe Zuberoan (Souletin) Basque with default penultimate stress plus a lexically marked class of final-stressed words, so the only open point is the label: Hualde (2003) calls this contrastive accent, while Hualde's own 1997 typology files Zuberoan with Polish and Finnish as a penultimate edge-counting system with lexical exceptions; the other systems reported for other dialects (Northern Bizkaian pitch accent in Elordieta & Selkirk 2018 and Ito 2002, Gipuzkoan in de Rijk 1972) are dialect variation, not contradiction.
variants.note: Zuberoan (Souletin) Basque, the eastern dialect of Basque spoken in Zuberoa/Soule; Hualde 2003 sec. 2.2.4 'Zuberoan' (penultimate accent with a marked final-accent class). Glottolog basq1250 Souletin, level dialect, parent basq1248 Basque (level language, iso eus).

44.dq: (11) Word Stress — Stress the initial syllable of a word. This rule is inviolable.
44.srule: Hayes & Lahiri 1991 give no secondary stress inside simple words; only in compounds: strongest stress on the compound-initial syllable, possibly a weaker stress on the initial syllable of the second member ('hard to hear', p. 55). Khan 2008 adds: secondary phonological stress often on all odd-numbered syllables after the initial one, extremely variable and sensitive to word-internal morpheme boundaries (sec. 6.4 p. 25 with fn. 12).

morph.src: Main source: Ray, Punya Sloka, Muhammad Abdul Hai & Lila Ray. 1966. Bengali Language Handbook. Washington: Center for Applied Linguistics (ERIC ED012914; xiii+137 pp.; ch.4 Verb words, ch.5 Noun words, ch.6 Auxiliary words, ch.7-8 phrases/clauses). Stress: Hayes, Bruce & Aditi Lahiri. 1991. Bengali intonational phonology. NLLT 9:47-96 (section 3 'Bengali stress', pp.55-57) [the reference our E=LEFT coding rests on]; supplementary: Khan, Sameer ud Dowla. 2008. Intonational Phonology and Focus Prosody of Bengali. UCLA PhD dissertation, ch.2 section 6 'Stress' pp.21-31.
morph.rootq: Hayes & Lahiri 1991:55 (section 3, rule 11): 'For Bengali, word stress follows a very simple rule (cf. Chatterji 1921, Klaiman 1987): (11) Word Stress: Stress the initial syllable of a word. This rule is inviolable. Compound words also have their strongest stress on their initial syllables. There may also be a weaker stress on the initial syllable of their second member, but this is hard to hear.'…
morph.elicq: Hayes & Lahiri 1991:48: 'Our data are based on Lahiri's speech, checked against that of three other native speakers of Calcutta Bengali.' and pp.56-57: 'A final caveat: stress in Bengali is usually quite weak phonetically, sometimes to the point of being almost inaudible. Our stress rules are supported by two types of evidence. First, in emphatic speech, the stresses are stronger and more audible, and occur where the rules above predict. Second, the stress rules are supported by the internal coherence that they provide to the intonational system: all of the various intonational contours we discuss below link up to texts in essentially the same way.'…
morph.stmt: Ray, Hai & Ray 1966 describe Bengali inflection as exclusively suffixing: 'The verb word is analyzable into a stem and a suffix' (§4, p.21; 50 verb suffixes VS-1..VS-50, no verbal prefixes) and 'A noun word is analyzable into an obligatory stem, followed optionally by an augment, followed optionally by a determiner suffix, followed optionally by a case suffix' (§5, p.35); the only prefixes are derivational noun/adjective prefixes that 'occur in only a few words' (/a- be- na- ni-/) or come with Sanskrit loans (/O- On- Su-/) (§5.4.3-5.4.4, p.37-38).

evidence_works.detail: The Tripura variety (Das 2001) is classed as ternary from the left edge with the leftmost stress primary, final syllables never stressed, and a binary foot used only to avoid two unfooted syllables. The entry describes standard Bengali (Hayes & Lahiri 1991) with initial stress: the initial primary agrees, the ternary secondary rhythm is specific to this variety and absent from the entry; Tripura Bangla has no Glottocode of its own in the catalog name index, so it is filed under Bengali.

corr.head: StressTyp2 codes a fixed pattern that its source does not state
corr.detail: StressTyp2 codes penultimate primary stress with alternating secondaries from the right, citing Kouwenberg 1994. The describer's 2013 summary conditions main stress on the shape of the final syllable (final stress for most CVN-final simplex words, penultimate when the final syllable is open) and notes a class of trisyllabic words with irregular initial stress; the 1994 grammar treats penultimate stress as the regular pattern, with stress on alternate syllables in polysyllabic words, and files these cases as irregular stress. The catalog keeps the penultimate rule and records these classes as exceptions.

45.dloc: Kouwenberg 2013, APiCS Online survey ch. 28 section 4.3 (https://apics-online.info/surveys/28, read); Kouwenberg 1994 Google Books id 322pIWa4WdQC excerpt fetched: p.289 'regular pattern of penultimate stress, and those that have an irregular stress pattern'; p.285 'emphatic stress and/or lengthening of the stress-bearing syllable in words which carry sentential stress, i.e. main verbs, nouns and adjectives'
45.heavy: A final syllable of the form CVN (closed by a nasal) attracts main stress to the final syllable in 'most' simplex words; an open final syllable leaves the default penult. No vowel-length contrast is invoked; word-final closed syllables in the language are essentially nasal-final only (K1994:294 excerpt: 'We find word-final closed syllables only in the following cases: (i) Words may end in a nasal consonant'). The 1994 grammar files the same final-/n/ words under 'irregular stress' while noting that 'it is not the case that irregular stress may be correlated with certain patterns of syllable structure'.
45.dflt: penultimate ('where the final syllable is open, the default placement of main stress in simplex words is penultimate')
45.prule: 2013 (describer's summary): final stress for most simplex words whose final syllable is CVN; otherwise default penultimate main stress in simplex words; 'a number of' trisyllabic words have irregular initial stress. 1994 (primary, excerpt): p. 289 'Non-derived or monomorphemic words may be grouped into two categories: those that follow the regular pattern of penultimate stress... and those that have an irregular stress pattern. Irregular stress is assumed to follow from partly prespecified prosodic structure.' p. 290 'Irregular stress means, in the majority of cases, initial stress in a trisyllabic word. The cases of irregular stress are listed here: (i) A large group of trisyllabic words have initial stress, e.g. alala 'tongue', astwele... bimiti... [irregular stress] may be correlated with certain patterns of syllable structure. (ii) Trisyllabic words ending in /ingi/ have initial stress; these words are skelinggi... palinggi... stelinggi... ketinggi...; the latter shows alternation between [initial and] penultimate stress. (iii) A few other trisyllabic words show alternation between regular penultimate stress [and irregular initial stress]... (iv)... final /n/ have final stress, e.g. furstan 'understand', alen 'alone', adungkan 'hide (waiting for game)'. (v) A few other words have final stress, viz. manggjapu 'maroon' (a lexicalized plural form < *manggi-apu (run-PL)), sukuli/suku (term...' Also p. 283: '... penultimate stress) vs. ʃuku 'dear child' (with final stress)'.
45.srule: Rhythmic stress on alternate syllables in polysyllabic words, counted from the regular penultimate main stress (Kouwenberg 1994:289 'stress falls on alternate syllables', read at Google Books grade: direction, exhaustiveness and behaviour in CVN-final and initial-stress words not shown). Not mentioned in Kouwenberg 2013 sec. 4.3.

45.loc: Kouwenberg 2013 APiCS survey ch. 28, section 4.3 (web edition, unpaginated); Kouwenberg 1994 pp. 289-290 (excerpt)

morph.stmt: Kouwenberg 1994:229 (excerpt): 'Affixation is always suffixation in BD.' The bound inventory is small and entirely post-root — plural -apu, nominalizer -jɛ (suffix ~ phrasal enclitic), perfective -tɛ, imperfective -a(rɛ), plus reduplication analysed as suffixation of a copy (K1994:291 list (31); APiCS survey §6 Table 4, §9.1) — while tense, mood, habitual, negation, articles, possession and pronominal arguments are expressed by free particles/words (preverbal wa/ma/sa/das, clause-final ka, prenominal di, juxtaposition/ʃi, pronoun words incl. weak 3SG o).

morph.rootq: Dubert & Dubert 1973 §4.3 p.30: "Primary stress occurs on the last or second last syllable of a stem. A stressless word or morpheme following a stem with no stress, gains stress on the first syllable. Secondary stress is predictable on the first syllable of a word. It occurs on the first and every alternate syllable preceeding stressed syllables, and/or on every alternate syllable following a stressed syllable." (examples pair bare stems with stem+classifier: 'mango / 'mangobʌk, 'panu / 'panumʌlʌ, 'ngʌragi / 'ngʌragiyʌng, 'sibillak / 'sibillakpʌk). Biangai OPD (M. Dubert 1992): "Primary stress occurs on the last or second last syllable of the stem."
morph.elicq: 1973 §1 p.5: "For this second draft of Biangai Phonemic analysis, the Werewere dialect was used with Mandani and Saweramou as the main informants. ... The data was collected 1962-72." No statement of how stress was elicited; the stress examples (§4.3 pp.30-31) are isolated citation words (stem vs. stem+suffix pairs); 1973 §3.2.3 p.9 adds only "the second vowel in the sequence [ai, au] is never stressed."
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing/encliticising: "Affix classes are based on order of occurrence from the verb stem. There is one order of prefixes [negative na-] and there are four orders of suffixes [Direction, Aspect, Tense, Mood]" (1978 Words §3.4.2 pp.45a-46); nominal categories are carried by 24 classifier "suffixes or post-clitics occurring optionally on the noun, obligatorily on the last word of the Noun Phrase" plus NP-final relator/actor/possessive clitics (§3.1 pp.9-18); the only other prefixes are the limiter ma- on pronouns/demonstratives and the object markers n-/m-/y-, which are prefixed to vowel-initial ditransitive stems but suffixed to consonant-initial ones.

48.dq: De klemtoon valt regelmatig op de voorlaatste lettergreep, zeer zelden op de laatste. ... Woorden, die in de taal waaruit zij overgenomen zijn, tweelettergrepig zijn, maar in het Bim. drielettergrepig moeten worden, behouden gewoonlijk hun accent, zoo hebben bijv. putir ... mantari ... kòròma ... sapatu ... den klemtoon op de eerste lettergreep.
48.srule: Jonker 1896 (§5-6, pp. 13-14) states a secondary accent (nevenaccent): four-syllable words regarded as root words are pronounced somewhat as two words, main accent on the penult and a secondary accent on the first syllable (four-syllable prefix derivations of trisyllabic roots are pronounced as one word); five-syllable words always have the main accent on the penult and a secondary accent on the second syllable.

48.sec_rule: Secondary accent (nevenaccent) on the first syllable of four-syllable root words and on the second syllable of five-syllable words (main accent on the penult in both; such words are 'pronounced somewhat as two words'); a four-syllable word formed by a living prefix on a trisyllabic root is pronounced as one word. Nothing stated for words of two, three, or six and more syllables.

Vijflettergrepige woorden, als bijv. sambara-mbura ... hebben dus steeds het hoofdaccent op de voorlaatste, en een nevenaccent op de tweedelettergreep.

secx.sec_quote_tr: Words of four syllables that are regarded as root words are pronounced somewhat as two words, such that the main accent falls on the penultimate but a secondary accent on the first syllable. ... Five-syllable words, e.g. sambara-mbura ... thus always have the main accent on the penultimate and a secondary accent on the second syllable.

49.prule: In KLT the stress is overall on the last-but-one (penultimate) syllable (stressable monosyllables aside); a few words, usually compounds, are end-stressed (listed: some nouns and an adjective, present-tense situative forms of bezañ, 1st/2nd persons of conjugated prepositions, some adverbs/pronouns/prepositions, place-names with a monosyllabic last component); in Gwenedeg the stress is overall final.
49.srule: Not mentioned in Press 2009 (ch. 10 'Breton', Phonology, pp. 431-434; whole chapter consulted). Later: Kennard 2021 (Phonology 38, section 5.2, AAM p. 28-29) reports, after Sommerfelt 1921 (Saint-Pol-de-Léon) and Jackson 1967 (Tregerieg, 'not consistently reported'), a secondary stress on the first syllable of four-syllable words and on the second syllable of five-syllable words (penultimate main stress), i.e. two syllables before the primary; her right-to-left syllabic-trochee analysis predicts this, but her own recordings contain only a handful of words longer than three syllables (e.g. fourchetezenn /ˌfurʃɛˈteːzɛn/ 'fork') and she leaves it to further research.

morph.stmt: Breton inflection and derivation are predominantly suffixing on the radical – Press 2009:469 lists the person/tense/mood endings 'all added to the radical' and p.443 'The plural is formed by endings, e.g. penn – pennoù, internal change + endings..., internal change only..., and suppletives' – with a productive diminutive -ig and many nominalising suffixes (446-447), a smaller set of derivational prefixes (ad-, di-/dis-, ken-, peur-, em- 'Note that lenition is often caused', 467), and all preposed grammatical material (articles, possessive and object pronouns, negative ne, verbal particles a/e/o, reflexive en em) realised as proclitic particles that trigger initial consonant mutation…

morph.stmt: Exclusively pre-root morphology: 'In grammatical terms Bidayuh words may consist of a root alone, a stem that consists of a root plus one to three prefixes, two roots compounded or a root or stem reduplicated... Suffixes as such have not been identified. However, a few morphemes, essentially singular person-markers, can be attached to the end of some roots or stems... These morphemes are viewed here as post-clitics, not suffixes' (Rensch et al. 2012:92); for Bukar-Sadong specifically, verb morphology consists of the (often irregular) nasal prefix, the prefixes ngi-/ni-, the infix -in-, penult-vowel alternation and nasal harmony (Court 1977:1-3).

50.sec_rule: Court 1972: simple words carry one (final) stress; secondary stress arises in complex words -- compounds and reduplicates weak-strong (main stress on the second element), stem + enclitic pronoun strong-weak (main stress on the stem-final syllable, secondary on the enclitic: rəˈminəˌkuʔ 'my house', ˈɟɨːʔˌɲãh 'a while ago'). As 'one solution' Court also allows a secondary stress on syllable 3 (the antepenult) of trisyllables that show full vowel contrasts there (e.g. kudapaʔ), which StressTyp2 coded as 'secondary stress on the initial syllable'.
50.sec_quote: the complex word has more than one stressed syllable or nucleus. One nucleus will be more strongly stressed than the [...] other [...] (1) compound words, in which the second element has the main stress and (2) suffixed forms, in which it is the first element which carries the main stress. [p.91] [...] Mentu Land Dayak does not have much suffixation: it lacks derivational suffixation, and has only enclitic pronouns with secondary stress, e.g. [rəˈminəˌkuʔ] 'my house' [p.92; phonetic form as transcribed in StressTyp2 word 1729, the scan's scan being illegible here]

The only other stress remark is also word-based, not root-based: repeated aliga forms "occur with heavier stress on the final syllable -ga in contrast to the general pattern of penultimate word stress" (§7.2.3, p.124).
morph.elicq: The stress statement carries no indication of how it was established: "Penultimate word stress occurs very generally and usually coincides with high pitch on the stressed syllable." (p.3). The only statement about the evidential base is for the grammar as a whole: "The data consists of 85 texts collected during 30 months residence at Bubuamo village between 1971 and 1976 under the auspices of the Summer Institute of Linguistics." (p.1). Intonation contours (§1.1-1.5) are illustrated on text-coded clauses (e.g. NN 105), but stress itself is not tied to any elicitation frame or measurement.

morph.elicq: Glasgow 1981 p.64 gives no statement of the evidence base; the section lists isolated words/short forms ("The following are examples of stress placement. 'řima 'hold it' / "gu'řimaŋa 'he is holding it' / "angu'řimapa 'the owner' / 'wola 'long ago' / 'wola"wola 'sometime, anytime' ...") and one remark on speech style: "In deliberate or emphatic speech the primary stress may be postponed to the second root of the word, in which case the first root receives only secondary stress." Green 1987 p.2-4: "The area of phonology was not included in my study; a summary of the phonology and morphophonology, drawn from Glasgow 1981 and 1985, is given".
morph.stmt: Green 1987 p.1: "Burarra is a non-Pama-Nyungan, multiple-classifying, prefixing language spoken in Arnhem Land"; verb template §4.0 p.35: "PRONOMINAL-DIRECTION-V-RECIPROCAL-INTRANS-TENSE/STATUS-REALIS NEG-CIRCS" — i.e. all person/number/class/mood-set and directional marking is prefixal on verbs, noun class and the single (locative/instrumental) case are prefixal on nominals, the nominaliser gu- is a prefix, while tense/status, realis negation -rna, valency-decreasing -ya/-chi- and subordinating -pa are suffixes (and free-pronoun case -pa/-la is suffixal).

52.sec_rule: Placed by morphology (Glasgow 1981:64): in prefixed words a secondary 'word attack' stress on the word-initial syllable (the prefix), primary being root-initial ("gu'řimaŋa, "angu'řimapa); in compound and reduplicated words a secondary stress on the first syllable of the second root ('wola"wola 'sometime, anytime', ŋu'bala"buŋgabiya 'my eyelids are drooping'); in emphatic speech, if primary moves to the second root, the first root keeps secondary stress (ŋu"bala'buŋgabiya). No rhythmic/alternating secondary stress is described.

evidence_works.detail: Eight speakers of Burarra/Gun-nartpa show a higher, flatter f0 peak and a small intensity rise on the word-initial syllable, but no significant vowel lengthening under stress, and onset lengthening only in glides and nasals. The study codes the first orthographic-word syllable as stressed, whereas the catalog's Glasgow 1981 entry puts primary stress on the first syllable of the first root after prefixes, so the two are not aligned on prefixed words; this DOI is already in the Burarra bibliography.

53.dq: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. Stress is not affected by the addition of suffixes or enclitics, such as the phrase-level plural marker /-ro/, or by the addition of paragogic /e/.. (Grimes 1995)
53.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (Grimes 1995 sec. 2.1). Syllabic enclitics such as the plural marker -ro and the paragogic /e/ are not counted, so host+enclitic forms carry stress on the host's penult ('ana-'fehu-ro, antepenultimate of the string); cliticised roots in tight phrases and compounds lose word stress (tub-'haa-t).

55.srule: Secondary stress on each alternating mora counting forwards and backwards from the main (stem-initial) stress within the word; in mid-sentence words the alternation is 'only virtually present', at the end of a sentence or paragraph it emerges clearly and the last secondary rises almost to a primary ('emphatic' pattern) (Seiler 1970:12).
55.quote: In addition, there is an accentual peculiarity which, no doubt, contributes to the marking of paragraph and sentence boundaries. The accentual scheme of isolated words is as follows: the main stress occurs in a fixed place — mostly on the first syllable of the stem; on each alternating mora counting forwards and backwards within the word we perceive a secondary stress, differing in loudness and pitch height from the primary stress. With words occurring in the middle of a paragraph or sentence the alternating stress pattern is only virtually present.

Verbs in TMD Cahuilla, which exhibit the highest degree of morphological complexity in the language and are head-marking, may have up to three prefix slots and four suffix slots" (Huaute 2023 p.227-228), and "maximally inflected nouns take, at most, one prefix and four suffixes" (p.254): person indexing (object, subject, possessor) and the reflexive tax- are prefixal, while tense-aspect-mood, causative/benefactive/motion derivation, number, case/postpositions and all nominalisers are suffixal; distributive/plural also use stem-initial CV- reduplication and vowel lengthening.

55.sec_rule: Secondary stress on every alternating mora counting both forwards and backwards from the main stress within the word (bidirectional, mora-counting: a long vowel counts two); sentence-medially the alternation is 'only virtually present', sentence/paragraph-finally the last secondary rises almost to a primary ('emphatic'). [Later: Huaute 2022:255; 2023:167, 323, own data on present-day Torres-Martinez Desert Cahuilla, finds only one level of stress and no evidence of secondary stress.]
55.sec_quote: on each alternating mora counting forwards and backwards within the word we perceive a secondary stress, differing in loudness and pitch height from the primary stress. With words occurring in the middle of a paragraph or sentence the alternating stress pattern is only virtually present. But at the end of a paragraph or sentence the pattern emerges clearly in performance

morph.rootq: OKMA grammar, cap. Fonología 'Acento' (pp.21-22): 'El Kaqchikel se caracteriza por tener acento fijo en una sílaba determinada. El acento es agudo, lo que significa que la acentuación siempre va a recaer en la sílaba final de la palabra (radical, derivada o compuesta por dos raíces unidas o dos palabras separadas). Al agregar enclíticos a los verbos y estativos (como direccionales), el acento tiende a caer sobre éstos.' (Examples: radical koyopa', derived tz'ib'anem, with enclitic xb'eruya' kan.) Consistent with p.90: 'la ocurrencia de vocal relajada, en palabras polisilábicas, es en sílaba final. La vocal relajada cambia a tensa cuando se le agrega un sufijo de derivación ... o de flexión…
morph.elicq: The OKMA grammar gives no statement of how stress was determined (rule plus word lists only). Bennett 2018 fn.7 rests the claim on phonotactic distribution rather than elicitation: 'There are two phonotactic patterns which diagnose stress in Kaqchikel: the presence of lax vowels, and the presence of a [ʔC] cluster. These are absolutely limited to stressed, word-final syllables ... Secondary stress has never been reported for Kaqchikel'. (An instrumental production/perception study exists — Berinstein 1979, UCLA WPP 47, already in the target's refs — but it was not the source used here.)
morph.stmt: Inflection is predominantly prefixal and derivation predominantly suffixal: 'La mayor parte de la flexión se presenta por medio de prefijos, existiendo algunos sufijos para determinadas funciones... posesión (prefijo) y pluralidad (sufijo) con sustantivos... tiempo/aspecto, modo, persona y número gramatical, y dirección con verbos, a través de prefijos (excepto los direccionales); también existen algunos sufijos que complementan los tiempos/aspectos y modos o indican categoría de los verbos' (p.77); 'La mayoría de los afijos derivacionales son sufijados a la raíz o base (sufijos) y solamente algunos son prefijados (der + Raíz, como aj-q'ij)' (p.89).

morph.stmt: Predominantly prefixing: person markers for possessor, intransitive subject and object are 'prefixados a um núcleo lexical (Nome, Verbo, Posposição)' (Castro Alves 2004:82), relational prefixes j-/ɲ-/tʃ-, middle pi-, detransitivizer aw- and the causative proclitic tɔ= all precede the root ('Os padrões derivacionais incluem verbos ou clíticos... prefixados a uma raiz verbal', p.78), while TAM, mood, negation and interrogation are free particles/clause-final operators ('Não há morfemas de tempo, aspecto e modo afixados no verbo', p.64); the only post-root bound material is the nominalizers -kate/-tʃɜ, noun class terms (-re DIM, -ti AUG, -kɜ, -hi...), the enclitics =ket/=pej/=je and the…

58.dq: Cavineña has a pitch-accent system where only pitch is relevant while length and intensity play no role. The accentual system is not contrastive though. Its role is to delimitate the phonological word as a prosodic domain. A phonological word receives a particular pitch contour which makes use of two pitch levels

58.srule: StressTyp2 (< Key 1968:25, not seen first-hand; StressTyp2's wording is 'are reported'): secondary stresses on alternating syllables leftward of the penultimate primary, i.e. even-numbered syllables from the right (maˌtohaˈiwa, aˌtataˈwaha). Liccardi 1983:67 notes only that 'algunos acentos secundarios' are marked in text transcriptions of long words, without placement.

58.exq_: interjections are phonologically irregular. For example, the interjection achí 'speaker feels disgusted' has a low-pitch-high-pitch contour; if it were regular, it would have the high-pitch-low-pitch contour normally applied to two syllable words (see §2.7).
58.tone: Guillaume 2008 §2.7 analyses Cavineña word prosody as a non-contrastive, word-delimiting pitch accent: the first syllable of the phonological word is High (spreading rightward), the last two syllables Mid (only the last in disyllables), formula Hn(M)M; 'only pitch is relevant while length and intensity play no role'. His 2024 handbook chapter calls it 'a mixed stress-tone accent system'. The SIL descriptions (Liccardi 1983:7; Camp & Liccardi 1989:267; Key 1968:25 as reported by StressTyp2) instead report penultimate stress, Liccardi 1983:8 also noting a word-initial high tone falling to mid over the rest of the word.

morph.rootq: "Cavineña differs from the other Takanan languages in having a mixed stress-tone accent system. As described by Guillaume (2008a: 41ff), the system operates as follows: (i) the first syllable of a phonological word receives a high pitch, (ii) the last two syllables receive a mid-pitch (only the last syllable in two-syllable words), and (iii) the high pitch of the first syllable extends rightward to any syllable(s) preceding the last two syllables. (A low pitch occurs on the last syllable(s) of an uttarence.) ... béta 'two', mátuja 'yacare caiman', jútákiju 'therefore', íwárá-kware call-REM.PST, kwéjá-méré-kware tell-CAUS-REM.PST." (Guillaume, Takanan languages, §2, ms p.9). Also: "The…
morph.elicq: "Takanan languages have complex and still poorly understood accentual systems. ... As described by Guillaume (2008a: 41ff), the system operates as follows: ..." (§2, ms pp.8-9). The chapter gives isolated citation words (béta, mátuja, jútákiju, íwárá-kware, kwéjá-méré-kware) plus one utterance-level remark ("A low pitch occurs on the last syllable(s) of an uttarence") but does not state what kind of data (wordlist, frames, texts, instrumental) the description rests on; Haude's review adds only "Pitch accent marks word boundaries."
morph.stmt: Cavineña is predominantly suffixing and encliticizing: the Takanan verbal template (Figure 10.3) has one TAM/mood prefix slot (-3: e-, pa-, ne-) and one valency prefix slot (-2: ka-) against five post-root slots (+2 valency, +3/+5 'adverbial', +4, +6 TAM), "the inflectional affixes... fill the most external slots, that is, -3, +4, and +6"; "only verbs can take verbal affixes (nouns have very little morphology)" — nouns take only the dummy/possessor prefix e- plus enclitics for number (=kwana, =ekatse), case (=ra, =ja, =ju, =eke, =tsewe) and kin possessor (=ke), and pronouns are "a root that expresses person (1, 2, 3) and up to three suffixes".
